hops.title: Pulse oximeters and skin pigmentation
hops.text: A fingertip pulse oximeter never touches your blood. It shines light through the skin and turns what comes out into an oxygen number, a proxy first developed in populations that were not racially diverse. In 2005, three commercial oximeters tested against arterial blood all overestimated low oxygen in volunteers with dark skin. In 2020, Michael Sjoding and colleagues checked 10,789 paired readings from Michigan hospital patients. When the clip read 92 to 96%, a true arterial saturation below 88% was missed in 11.7% of readings from Black patients and 3.6% from White patients. Only checking the clip against arterial blood revealed the gap.

sources.citation: Sjoding MW, Dickson RP, Iwashyna TJ, Gay SE, Valley TS. Racial Bias in Pulse Oximetry Measurement. N Engl J Med. 2020;383(25):2477-2478.
Bickler PE, Feiner JR, Severinghaus JW. Effects of skin pigmentation on pulse oximeter accuracy at low saturation. Anesthesiology. 2005;102(4):715-719.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: An open fingertip pulse oximeter glowing softly red on a wooden table beside a closed notebook.
image.caption: A light-based reading is only as good as the checks against the real thing.

hops.title: Six spike sorters, one recording
hops.text: Give one recording to six spike-sorting programs and you might expect six similar neuron counts. In 2020, Alessio Buccino and colleagues tried it on a 15-minute Neuropixels recording from a mouse at the Allen Institute, with 246 active channels. Tridesclous found 187 units. SpyKING Circus found 628, more than three times as many. The team then compared the spike timing of every unit across programs. Even under what the authors called relatively undemanding matching criteria, all six agreed on just 33 units. For most sorters, over half of their units matched no other sorter at all.

sources.citation: Buccino AP, Hurwitz CL, Garcia S, Magland J, Siegle JH, Hurwitz R, Hennig MH. SpikeInterface, a unified framework for spike sorting. eLife. 2020;9:e61834.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Six computer monitors wired to one silicon probe, each displaying a different pattern of colored dot clusters.
image.caption: Six sorting programs read the same probe recording and agreed on only 33 units.

hops.afterHeading: Atlases and connectomes: steps the data do not fully check
hops.title: Signals the worm's wiring map does not show
hops.text: It is tempting to think a complete synapse map would tell you how signals flow. In 1986, John White, Sydney Brenner and colleagues published a wiring map of most of the nervous system of the 302-neuron roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans: about 5,000 chemical synapses and 600 gap junctions. In 2023, Francesco Randi and colleagues at Princeton activated single head neurons with light across 23,433 neuron pairs while imaging calcium. Signals spread differently from what a model based on the wiring map predicted. Some signaling depended on dense-core vesicles, sometimes in under a second, often between neurons with no direct wired connection. The authors propose that neuropeptides released outside synapses are responsible.

sources.citation: White JG, Southgate E, Thomson JN, Brenner S. The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci. 1986;314(1165):1-340.
Randi F, Sharma AK, Dvali S, Leifer AM. Neural signal propagation atlas of Caenorhabditis elegans. Nature. 2023;623(7986):406-414.

image.caption: Some worm neurons respond quickly to partners with no direct connection on the wiring map.

audio.title: Three surprises inside big brain datasets
audio.transcript:
Big numbers in neuroscience sound solid. Here are three true stories in which the measurement itself surprised the people holding it.

First, spike sorting. When a silicon probe sits in a brain, software has to decide which small electrical blips belong to which neuron. In two thousand four, Frank Wood and colleagues gave human sorters synthetic recordings where the right answer was already known. Even human sorters averaged twenty-three percent false positives and thirty percent false negatives. Software should settle that, you might think. In twenty twenty, Alessio Buccino and colleagues ran six modern spike-sorting programs on the same fifteen-minute mouse Neuropixels recording. One program found one hundred eighty-seven units. Another found six hundred twenty-eight, more than three times as many, from the very same file. When the researchers compared the timing of the spikes each program grouped together, all six agreed on just thirty-three units. A sorted unit is an estimate, not a guaranteed single cell.

Second, the glowing mouse. Transgenic mouse lines that make their own calcium sensor are wonderfully convenient: the mice make the sensor in selected neurons themselves, with no virus to inject. Then in twenty seventeen, Nicholas Steinmetz and collaborators across four laboratories reported something odd. In sixty-three of one hundred seventy-five mice, the imaging showed large flashes sweeping across parts of the cortex, especially in certain widely used lines. Electrical recordings picked up large spikes resembling those seen between epileptic seizures. Yet many neuronal responses and behaviors seemed normal. In one affected line, the team added doxycycline to the drinking water to hold off making the sensor until the mice were seven weeks old. During follow-up, those flashes did not appear in the part of the cortex they imaged. The mechanism is still unclear, but the point is uncomfortable: even a glowing reporter may change the very circuit you built it to observe.

Third, wiring diagrams. For more than forty years, researchers including Eve Marder have studied a tiny circuit of about thirty neurons in the crab's stomach. It drives the stomach's rhythms, including the gastric mill rhythm that chews food. The wiring is among the best mapped in biology. Yet bathe that same circuit in different neuromodulators and it produces different rhythms. The wires stay put while the chemistry changes what they do. The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans makes the same point. In nineteen eighty-six, researchers published a wiring map of most of its nervous system: three hundred two neurons and roughly five thousand chemical synapses. In twenty twenty-three, Princeton researchers stimulated single head neurons across twenty-three thousand four hundred thirty-three pairs while imaging the whole brain. Some neurons responded to partners with no direct wired connection, some signals arrived in less than a second, and the results point to neuropeptides drifting outside synapses.

Sorting programs, a glowing mouse, a crab's stomach and a worm all point the same way. Every big brain number is a proxy, and the interesting discoveries often begin when someone tests the step between what was measured and what it was hoped to mean.
